item.title: 6 More Things I've Learned as a Therapist
item.description:
Therapy

6 More Things I've Learned as a Therapist

Personal Perspective: A good therapist pays attention to details.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists should engage in good self-care so they can be fully present.
  • Your therapist should remember who the important players in your life are.
  • Therapy should have clear goals, and these goals should be revisited.

This is Part 2 of a series. Read Part 1 here.

Over the decades, I have learned so much from my experiences in my consultation room, from my patients and from taking note of my own behavior as a therapist. I try to put my whole self into each session. My goal is to pay attention with my heart and brain. I remind myself to pay attention to verbal cues, body language, and the type of energy that clients are bringing into therapy (e.g., anxiety, frustration, dysphoria, etc.). My hope is that I will continue to grow as a therapist and that I will continue to do my best with the individuals I work with. I am also hoping that this post will inform therapists and their clients.

There are a number of points that I would like to add to my initial list:

  1. A good therapist is well-rested, well-nourished, and taking good care of his or her physical and mental health. I can't emphasize this strongly enough. First, if you are not engaging in good self-care, then I highly doubt that you can be fully present for your clients. And, yes, I have heard more than one story of a therapist falling asleep mid-session. Imagine the feeling that that engenders in someone who is opening up to you and assuming that you are very much available to help. Second, as a therapist, you are in a position to be an excellent role model. Please take that seriously.
  2. Keep excellent and thorough notes after the session while everything is still fresh in your mind. You should be able to refer back to themes, history, progress, medication usage, and those who people your clients' lives. Look at these notes prior to each session so that you can engage your clients fully without asking them to repeat themselves frequently.
  3. Review the goals of the therapy sessions regularly. Ask your client if they would like to continue with current goals, add new ones, or modify earlier goals. Therapy should have a clear focus that can be articulated by clients and patients. Rambling sessions don't serve anyone, although an occasional bit of rambling is inevitable. We all do it.
  4. Continue to educate yourself and stay up to date with current research and practices in your particular field. Yes, decades of experience are helpful, but new ideas and research are alive and well, and we should all be interested in learning about new models of care.
  5. Timing is everything. If you have been paying attention, then you will know when your clients are ready to discuss tricky topics. Here, I am especially thinking about having clients disclose family secrets. Tread gently and empathically. Explain that your office is a safe space and unburdening themselves of secrets might feel like a huge relief. This is especially important if individuals are carrying secrets that cause shame and/or embarrassment.
  6. Pay attention to what your clients avoid talking about. Perhaps they are avoiding discussion of someone or a situation that had a tremendous impact on them. What is avoided may be just as important as what is discussed.

item.title: What 'Prima Facie' Gets Right About Trauma and the Law
item.description:
Trauma

What 'Prima Facie' Gets Right About Trauma and the Law

Cynthia Erivo's latest film reveals the gap between trauma and justice.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Freezing, dissociation, and fragmented memory are survival mechanisms, not signs of unreliability.
  • Systemic failures often discourage survivors from reporting sexual violence and erode trust in authorities.
  • A healthy consent culture includes respecting "no" without force or pushback.

Note. Some spoilers may follow.

The September 2026 Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) hosted the world premiere of Prima Facie, a screen adaptation of the Tony Award- and Olivier Award-winning play of the same name. The film stars Oscar-nominated Cynthia Erivo as Tessa Ensler, a criminal defence barrister in the heart of London’s legal core, who has built a reputation for her skillful arguments and strong courtroom presence.

Tessa begins the film with immense trust in the criminal justice system and relies on the law to ensure the process, the rules, and the burden of proof hold up no matter who stands on which side. Jurisprudence sustains her faith in legal formalism, the belief that the law is objective, irrespective of broader social contexts, and helps her navigate the merciless and adversarial trials surrounding sexual assault and violent crime. This changes when she discovers how flawed and misogynistic the justice system is when she herself becomes the victim of rape, standing on the other side of the courtroom as one of the few women to speak up.

The film is brilliantly written and tactfully directed, weaving together themes of power, privilege, bias, and toxic masculinity, alongside the despair that follows a sexual assault socially, emotionally, and psychologically. The film depicts the sad reality of how survivors of rape are treated under the law, and whose voices disproportionately have the most power and influence. The movie has too many nuances to cover everything; however, a few things stand out.

How the Film Captures the Body's Response to Trauma

Tessa's experience of rape was a heart-wrenching watch, and the directorial and acting choices highlighted the complexities of trauma. The directorial and creative team uses the symbolism of broken glass to capture the sense of self-fragmentation that so often follows surviving a traumatic experience. White noise evokes dissociation, the survival response of detaching from one's bodily experience to endure unimaginable pain and suffering.

This supports the polyvagal theory of autonomic arousal, which in part suggests that when we cannot fight or flee from a threatening experience, our nervous system will decrease in arousal (or freeze), conserve bodily functions, and “prepare for death.” The physiological changes in this state allow the body to dampen pain and preserve energy, which can leave a person feeling numb, detached, or unable to move or speak. The stressful situation also affects a person’s ability to store and consolidate memories.

The internal process of a physiological trauma response is portrayed well, and the film also highlights how these natural survival instincts are weaponized both in and out of the courtroom to discredit women and survivors of sexual violence. While the criminal justice systems in Canada and the United Kingdom (UK) have some safeguards for survivors (for instance, the “rape shield” provision in Canada, which bars using a complainant's sexual history to suggest she was more likely to have consented or is less believable), the cross-examinations can often be used to discredit the survivors' experiences based on their recollections of memories or events. The film calls on courts to better understand the psychological and physiological impacts of surviving violence when adjudicating sexual assault cases.

Grief, Self-Doubt, and the Decision to Report

Erivo’s performance captured a rich internal struggle of grieving what was lost: her sense of self, trust, integrity, and relationships. This included her struggle to grapple with choosing to report her experience of being raped by a colleague to the authorities.

In the UK, where the film is set, approximately 1 in 4 women and 1 in 18 men experience a sexual assault. Yet 5 in 6 women and 7 in 8 men do not report these offences to the police. Similarly, in Canada, compared to physical assaults, sexual assaults are reported to police in only about 8.6 percent of cases.

Reporting a sexual assault can be a daunting and life-changing process, and as Tessa experienced, the adversarial nature of the criminal justice system is fundamentally flawed when it comes to sexual violence. This is part of why many survivors don't feel safe reporting their assaults to authorities. In a qualitative study of 23 survivors of sexual assault, 65 percent knew the perpetrator, much like Tessa. Many participants also did not receive follow-up from police after making a report, which discouraged them from reporting future sexual violence and eroded their trust in the justice system.

Other research highlights a tendency for people to disproportionately blame victims of rape when they are assaulted by a known individual or acquaintance compared to a stranger. Throughout the film, Tessa struggles with her own self-doubt, which is a common experience for survivors of sexual violence. She actively questions whether she should or shouldn’t report, and questions her own experiences, which is a natural response to trauma.

Tessa chose to report to the police, and that choice is not one every survivor makes or should feel obligated to make. Deciding not to report is not a sign of weakness; it is often a reasonable act of self-protection within a system that too often fails the people it is meant to serve. Yet stories like Tessa's remind us that speaking up, whether to a trusted friend, a therapist, or a courtroom, can be a powerful act of reclaiming one's voice. And every survivor who shares their experience, in whatever form feels safe, adds to a collective call for a justice system that believes, protects, and responds to survivors.

No Means No, and It Must Be Heard

In a live question-and-answer at TIFF, screenwriter Suzie Miller and star Cynthia Erivo shared their public advocacy for healthier masculinities that promote and respect women's autonomy and consent. Erivo spoke about people’s resistance to hearing the word “no,” stating, "No is no. And if I don't say yes, I still mean no." This is an important message for consent; however, in many cases, there may be fear of refusing sex or stating boundaries. As Erivo put it, "We have to address the way we react to the word 'no' so that we can actually say it comfortably and know that we will be listened to."

item.title: When You Don't Have a Map, Find Your Inner Compass
item.description:
Decision-Making

When You Don't Have a Map, Find Your Inner Compass

Four inner voices can help you find direction when a decision seems unclear.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Difficult decisions often involve four distinct voices: desire, fear, obligation, and the deeper self.
  • The loudest inner voice is not necessarily the wisest; each voice offers insight and potential distortion.
  • Separating competing inner voices can reveal what each one knows, fears, protects, and values.
  • Discernment may not reveal the whole path, but it can provide enough clarity to take the next faithful step.

Not long ago, I faced what seemed like a defining career decision. Thirty-five years earlier, I had made a choice that changed the course of my professional life: I left a highly sought-after executive role at a large corporation to start my own business. At the time, a chorus of voices pushed back—many of them not my own. “Are you crazy? You’re walking away from the security, status, excitement, and financial rewards of being a senior vice president?” That was my mother’s voice, but other voices, including some within me, were just as loud and persuasive. Heck, I even had a corner office in a modern downtown skyscraper and a plant in the corner next to a huge window overlooking the city. In the end, I took the leap, and it became one of the best decisions of my life. But it was not an easy one.

Fast-forward to 2025, and it was time for another consequential choice that seemed about as important as the one I just described. This time it had to do with the shifting nature of the firm we had founded and built over those years, and my relationship with it. Hard as it may seem to realize for all of us, nothing lasts forever, and my business partners and I were getting to a point in our careers that called for a change. What would that change look like for the structure of the firm and our roles in relation to the firm we started and nurtured for all those years?

Source: SHVETS Production / Pexels

Please allow me to get to the essence of this post by describing the four voices that I noticed were speaking to me about this decision.

The first voice is that of “Desire.” It asks, “What do I want?” In this case, it represented information about the vitality, success, and positive feedback that I have always felt from my work and leadership of my firm.

The second voice is “Fear,” which asks, “What am I trying to protect?” In this case, I was likely thinking about my identity for 25 years, and the fear I felt at the thought of ending this monumental achievement in my life.

Third is the voice of “Obligation,” which asks, "What do I believe I am supposed to do?" I might be letting others down, for example, or I may feel an obligation to continue serving my longstanding clients.

Lastly, the fourth voice is that of the “Deeper Self,” and it is concerned with the sense of mission, values, and overall congruence of one’s life. For me, what seemed to matter most was legacy and adding value to others, and the future of our clients and their positive impact on the world.

At this point, to shed more light on the challenge that the four voices bring as it relates to decision-making and discernment, we can circle back to the subtitle of this post for further clarification. The fact is that each of the four voices, and what they represent in our lives, offers unique value in our decision process. This is where discernment and deep listening enter the equation, and when we might find ourselves mistaking the loudest voice for the wisest. Often, the feelings of urgency, anxiety, desire, and responsibility can each feel authoritative and definitive. The mistake lies not in having these voices but in not taking the time to understand them and see them as different parts of ourselves and then to listen carefully to what each has to offer us in the important, seemingly unresolvable decisions we face in our lives.

You can apply this to an unresolved decision for yourself, and here is how to approach it. First, put the unresolved decision at the top of a page and create four sections: Desire, Fear, Obligation, and Deeper Self. Then follow these steps;

  1. Write without editing for two minutes under each heading, working from this point of view and its attendant feelings, listing the messages that you are receiving.
  2. Circle repeated words or themes in each of the four areas of the page.
  3. Notice which voice is loudest, which is quietest, and which one holds the most power.
  4. Ask: What does each voice know? What does each voice distort? Where is the wisdom here, and what messages are most aligned with my highest self?
  5. Finish by engaging the voices in a discourse, a give-and-take, and see if you can come to a voice that accepts who you are and identifies what the faithful first step might be in this situation.

This process and disciplined discernment do not always produce certainty, but they can generate enough clarity for one responsible next move, which can take you on a road to further clarity.

To illustrate this point with a metaphor, think about the distinction between a map and a compass. We often want a decision to reveal the entire future, the entire map. Alternatively, we can put the focus on orienting ourselves and our direction, more like a compass: knowing which direction is more aligned with our truth and the person we are becoming. Perhaps we do not need the whole path at this point. We just need enough quiet to hear the voices within us, enough honesty to know which one is speaking, and enough courage to take the next faithful step, based on the revealed orientation of our internal compass.

Let me conclude by going back to the decision I described at the start of this post. I was able to give space for the first three voices using a process just as I described above. I discovered which voices were operating very loudly for me and why. But as I sat with it longer, the voices and their messages came together with a clear direction, as with the compass metaphor, and it became clear to me that the most important element of the decision was about continuing to bring my skills to the world, but in a different manner and working with a different set of clients, more with schools, not-for-profit organizations, and mission-driven companies. I made a decision to simplify the corporate structure of the company I’d created over 35 years ago by creating a simplified LLC legal entity. This entity had much of the same sense of mission and purpose but was simpler and more fluid, allowing me to focus on projects and people that hold great meaning for me at this stage of my life, and allowing me more flexibility and creativity to spread my wings and live into my legacy.

item.title: Hyperreligious Delusions During Psychosis
item.description:
Psychosis

Hyperreligious Delusions During Psychosis

Personal Perspective: When psychotic delusions turn faith against you.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Delusions can deeply distort faith, making it feel like a source of danger instead of comfort.
  • Many experience hyperreligious delusions but often feel isolated and alone in them.
  • While faith may be a liability during these breaks, it may also be key to spiritually surviving psychosis.
Source: Marco / Adobe Stock

Many of my delusions and associated hallucinations revolved around classic narratives of schizophrenia: I thought my hospital room was bugged with surveillance, I thought someone was controlling my mind, and I thought there was a conspiracy to kill me. Common and less talked about, however, are hyperreligious delusions.[1] The American Psychological Association defines them as “any delusion associated with religious beliefs and grandiose ideas with religious content. Delusional ideation frequently includes beliefs that the individual is the embodiment of a notable religious figure, such as a messiah or prophet, and that they possess special powers, such as the ability to cure all illness.”[2] Examples of my hyperreligious delusions include: being put to life-threatening tests by God to prove my faith; thinking I’m the Antichrist; and drawing a demon on paper, losing its grip on me and falling into the abyss in an art class on the ward.

I spoke on a panel at an annual conference for the National Alliance on Mental Illness North Carolina a few years ago on the topic of spirituality and mental illness.[3] I mentioned that I had hyperreligious breaks, and a woman came up to me and said that it meant everything to her that I brought that up because she agreed that no one talks about them.

My Faith Used Against Me

I grew up in the church, and for most of my life, I have been a devout Christian. It’s impossible not to wonder: Is it because I was already religious that I was capable of having such hyperreligious delusions, or can they happen to anyone? In ways, having so many hyperreligious delusions felt like my faith had betrayed me and worked against me. It was as if I was punished for being a person of faith.

My hyperreligious delusions even had me cross a busy intersection without looking to prove my faith. I also got lost in the dark without a coat in December, trying to follow my spiritual path with my feet. In these experiences, I had to prove how strong my faith was and whether I really believe in God enough, but it resonates now like a cruel joke. It has made me question how valuable and true my faith can be if it could be turned against me like that.

On the other hand, while my faith was betrayed by my psychotic mind, it has been my faith in God that has afforded me the infinite patience to allow time to heal me both cognitively and emotionally. So, while my faith was used against me to bring me harm and even potentially kill me, in many ways, it is my faith that I have credited during my recovery for my emotional and spiritual survival.

Making Sense of Hyperreligious Delusions and Their Relationship to Authentic Faith

I’ve had a very painful life, where my psychotic breaks are just one source of pain that was probably the result or outcome of major early traumas that caused my complex PTSD and psychotic disorder. I’ve turned to faith for every single trauma and pain in my life, basically throwing myself into faith for survival. I’ve sought faith despite having doubts and frustration with God at the same time. The fact that my faith could be turned against me by my own brain to try to kill me instead of save me is the greatest mystery and the cruelest component of my entire illness.

The fact that antipsychotics made the hyperreligious delusions go away means I had an objective, medical issue that has nothing to do with who I am as a person or what I believe in terms of faith. Antipsychotics' effectiveness also separates those incidents from my real relationship with God and helps me move forward with a faith that I know is truly authentic instead of being a sham. Even though I put my life on the line several times when my faith was twisted and distorted, I know I can put my whole heart into faith moving forward now.

My Thoughts for You if You’ve Experienced the Same Thing

First of all, you are not alone. It’s easy to think that you are the only person in the world who has experienced certain types of delusions until you have the opportunity to find community and exchange experiences. It may be hard to believe, but I know many people who have thought they were the Antichrist, and it means so much to people, including myself, to realize that is a typical delusion, even though it sounds way too specific and bizarre to be common.

As I wrote in a previous post, your delusions and hallucinations are not yours to own and do not necessarily reflect on you as a person or your beliefs. After your illness, there is no need for you to explain the content of your hyperreligious delusions unless it would be meaningful for you. It does not do yourself or others good to judge yourself or your faith journey. If you are a person of faith in a religion, I do believe there could be a pathway forward in your religious tradition afterwards, if you want there to be.

My Choice to Believe Anyway

We cannot help but wonder if faith is anything greater than a mechanism in our brain if our faith can be distorted and used against us in these ways, especially if you are not a person of faith but have had hyperreligious delusions anyway. Faith is a matter of personal choice for everyone, despite the many reasons to have doubts and the complete inability to prove its validity one way or the other.

For me personally, I have chosen to believe anyway on the other side of my breaks, even though this pathway back towards faith has not always been intuitive, direct, or easy. Even though faith seemed like both poison and cure for me, I now know my faith to be authentic and true now that my illness is in remission. Even though hyperreligious delusions could have easily ended my life, I would not be here today or be a writer and speaker on mental illness without my faith in a higher power.

My Book on Faith and Suffering

If you are interested in reconciling your faith with suffering, I just published a book of faith-based sonnets called My Soul to Keep: Faith in the Midst of Suffering Leads to Deliverance and Praise by Prolific Pulse Press.[4] This book functions like a spiritual memoir and is available for online purchase on a number of major platforms.
